analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and pays for it with new taxes on income above $250,000 and investment gains.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security benefits across the board, eventually by 15%, switch inflation adjustments to an index that tracks what seniors actually buy, set a minimum benefit at the poverty level for people who worked long careers at low wages, and let children in school collect benefits until age 22. To pay for it, it would apply the Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income above $250,000 — today, wages above about $133,000 are exempt — and triple the tax on high-income investment gains from 3.8% to 10%. It would also merge the retirement and disability trust funds into one.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future retirees, disabled workers, and survivors, who would see benefits rise gradually to 15% above current levels. Lifetime low earners would get the biggest lift: a minimum benefit tied to the federal poverty line, scaled up by years worked, so someone with 30+ years in the workforce would get at least 125% of the poverty guideline. Seniors would get slightly larger annual inflation adjustments under a price index built for elderly consumers. Children of retired, deceased, or disabled workers who stay in school full-time could collect benefits through age 22 instead of 18–19, and Railroad Retirement beneficiaries would get the same extension. The program's long-term financing gap would shrink because the new taxes on high earners and investment income flow into the trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, and low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises benefits for new beneficiaries by 1 percentage point a year starting in 2025, reaching a 15% increase in 2039 and after.
Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, an inflation measure built on the spending patterns of households age 62 and older.

Creates a new minimum benefit: a lifetime low earner with 11 to 30 or more years of work would be guaranteed a benefit scaled from 6.25% up to 125% of the federal poverty guideline for a single individual, with existing benefits recomputed upward.

Lets children of retired, deceased, or disabled workers who are full-time students keep receiving benefits until age 22 instead of losing them around age 18–19, with the same change made to the Railroad Retirement program.

Funds the expansion and improves solvency by applying the Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment earnings above $250,000 (the 2019 cap was $132,900) and raising the net investment income tax on high-income taxpayers from 3.8% to 10%, with 62% of that investment tax dedicated to the trust fund.
Merges the retirement and disability trust funds into a single Social Security Trust Fund.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and investors. Employees and employers would pay Social Security payroll tax on wages above $250,000, which are currently exempt beyond the annual cap (about $133,000 in 2019); self-employed people would pay it on earnings above that level as well. Individuals above the income thresholds would pay a 10% tax on net investment income, up from 3.8% — this falls on capital gains, dividends, and other investment returns of higher-income filers. Under the bill's text, income above the $250,000 line is taxed without a corresponding increase in those earners' benefit formula, so the tax is a financing measure, not added earnings credit.

drawbacks.text: The tax falls almost entirely on the top: wages and self-employment earnings above $250,000 and investment income of high-income taxpayers would carry new or higher taxes, and the bill text provides no corresponding benefit-formula credit for earnings above that line, so those filers pay without added accrual.

Tripling the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 10% would raise the tax cost of investment returns, an objection critics of capital taxation would raise on grounds of savings and investment incentives.

The across-the-board increase phases in slowly — 1% in 2025 rising to 15% by 2039 — so today's beneficiaries see little of the headline expansion for years, and the $250,000 threshold is fixed in the statute, not indexed to future wage growth.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people the bill serves — retirees, disabled workers, and lifetime low earners — the gains are large and concrete, especially the poverty-level minimum benefit and the more senior-accurate inflation index. The cost is borne by a narrow, affluent group through payroll and investment taxes, which is the honest tradeoff the bill is built to make: an explicit transfer of financing from high earners to benefit expansion and solvency. A fair criticism is design, not direction: the slow phase-in and the fixed $250,000 threshold mean the bill as written would deliver less and tax slightly differently than a fully indexed version would.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it never reached the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on February 13, 2019, with four Democratic cosponsors: Gillibrand, Merkley, Booker, and Harris.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, no floor vote — for the remainder of the 116th Congress.
The Finance Committee, chaired by a Republican senator, held the bill's fate; under Senate practice a committee chair decides whether a referred bill ever gets scheduled for consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income taxpayers and investors are better off because the bill died: the new payroll tax above $250,000 and the 10% investment income tax never took effect. Incumbent senators also never had to cast a vote on a large benefit expansion paired with a tax increase on top earners.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and investors who avoided new taxes

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security Expansion Act and sponsored it in the Senate.

for.name: 4 Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all four signed on at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral; chair Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or report — leaving the bill unconsidered for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor caucuses with Democrats and all four cosponsors were Democrats; no Senate Republican cosponsored or acted on the bill, and with the chamber's Republican-led Finance and floor leadership taking no action it never came to a vote.

industries.note: The bill's financing comes from this group: payroll tax on wages and self-employment income above $250,000 and a tripling of the net investment income tax to 10%. The bill's gains for beneficiaries are this group's cost.

industries.industry: Social Security beneficiaries (retirees, disabled workers, survivors, students)
industries.note: Not an industry but the bill's core constituency: across-the-board increases, a poverty-level minimum benefit for long-career low earners, CPI-E inflation indexing, and extended student-child benefits through age 22.
